title: The Blue Mug
subject: rla
passage:
Every morning before opening the bakery, Mara placed a chipped blue mug beside the register. It never held coffee. Pens collected in it, along with a pair of scissors and the small metal key to the delivery door.

When Theo started working there, he assumed the mug was simply another object no one had bothered to replace. On his third day, he lifted it while wiping the counter. "We could use something cleaner," he said.

Mara looked up so quickly that Theo set it down. "That one stays."

She did not explain. The mug remained, blue glaze worn pale along the handle, while everything around it changed. New menu boards replaced the handwritten ones. A brighter display case arrived. Theo learned which customers wanted their bread sliced thin and which wanted the darkest loaves.

The bakery was not sentimental about most things. A bent tray was recycled. A cracked plastic container went into the trash. When a supplier sent a box of matching utensil cups, Mara replaced three mismatched jars without hesitation. The blue mug alone remained beside the register. Theo noticed the exception but stopped asking about it. He began to think of the mug as part of the bakery's routine, like the first batch of rolls cooling near the window or Mara checking the ovens twice before unlocking the door.

Months later, a pipe burst in the apartment above the bakery. Water ran through the ceiling before dawn, soaking boxes and spreading across the floor. Theo arrived to find Mara standing in the doorway, counting what could be saved. Her voice was practical - unplug the mixer, move the flour, call the landlord - but her hands shook when she reached the register.

Theo saw the blue mug on the floor. A crack had split it from the rim almost to the base. He picked it up carefully.

"My brother made that," Mara said. Her voice was smaller now. "First pottery class. He said the handle looked like an ear."

Theo looked at the awkward handle and, for the first time, saw that it really did. He also understood why the mug had survived every cleanup. Its chipped edge and uneven shape were not signs that no one had bothered to replace it. They were part of the reason Mara recognized it immediately as something that belonged to a particular person and time.

The bakery reopened four days later. The damaged mug could no longer hold pens, so Mara placed it on the shelf above the register. Theo found a plain metal cup for the scissors and keys. He did not suggest throwing anything away.
